lesson.title: Follow a value through a program

steps.headline: A line like price = 4 works out the right side now and stores the result under a name.

lead.text: Python runs one line at a time, from the top. An assignment stores a value, not a formula. Later lines can read the name, or store a new value under it.
A name does not remember how its value was calculated. Spreadsheets recalculate; Python does not.
The program stores total, then changes price. Think about what total was given when it was stored.

reveal.text: Whatever you predicted, Python worked out 5 × 4 once, at the line that stored total. Changing price later did not run that line again.

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6
total = price * 3

steps.headline: A notebook cell sets count = 2. Then a second cell, count += 3, is run twice. What is count?

lead.text: A notebook sends each cell you run to a kernel. The kernel keeps every name between runs until you restart it.

workedSteps.text: The first cell stores 2 under count.
Run the second cell once. count += 3 means count = count + 3.
Run it again. It starts from the value the kernel kept.

steps.headline: A notebook starts with count = 1. You run count += 4 three times. What is count at the end?

workedSteps.text: Start with count = 1. The first run adds 4.
The second run adds 4 to the kept value. What is count now?
The third run adds 4 again. What is count at the end?

lead.text: A line that starts with # is a comment. It is a note for readers.

reveal.text: The comment line never ran, so x stayed at the value it was given. Notes explain code; only statements change what the names hold.

lead.text: A notebook has three cells, run in this order: rate = 2, then total = rate * 10, then rate = 5.

reveal.text: Cell 2 read the rate the kernel held when it ran, which was the newest one. Restarting the kernel and running every cell in order is the check that a notebook does not depend on an old run.

lesson.orientation: Track assignment and execution order, then make a notebook reproducible.
lesson.reviewLabel: Follow a value through a program
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: In a spreadsheet, cell A1 holds 5 and cell B1 holds the formula =A1*4. Then you type 9 into A1.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow a value through a Python program line by line, and say what a notebook still remembers.

recap.keyIdea: A name holds the value it was given at that line. Python runs lines in order, and a notebook kernel keeps every name between runs.

blocks.text: You saw that total keeps 20 when price changes later. You found count at 13 after three runs, and that running cell 2 again reads the newest rate.

recap.nextHook: Next: what kind of value a name holds, and why '12' + '3' is not 15.

questions.prompt: Set price = 5, then total = price * 4, then price = 9. What value does total keep?
hints: Which value did price hold when total was stored?
total was stored before price changed.
Work out 5 × 4 once; the later assignment affects only price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: total was assigned 5 × 4 = 20. Reassigning price does not run the earlier multiplication again.

questions.onCorrect: 20. total stored the result of 5 × 4 at its own line; changing price afterwards left it alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That recalculates with the new price, as a spreadsheet would. Python stored total before the price changed.
That is the final price. The question asks what total keeps.

questions.prompt: What is count after the third run?
hints: Start from the value after the second run.
Add 4 once more.
Work out 9 + 4.
questions.onCorrect: 13. Three runs add 4 three times to the starting 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts three lots of 4 but forgets the starting 1.
That is the value after the second run. The third run adds 4 more.

questions.prompt: The program sets x = 3, then has the line # x = 50, then y = x * 2. What is y?
hints: Which of these lines does Python actually run?
A line starting with # is only a note.
Work out 3 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The comment is skipped, so x is 3 and y is 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The comment never ran, so x stayed 3. Only statements change what a name holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses x = 50. The line starting with # is a comment, so it never ran.
The comment did not run, so x is not 50.

questions.prompt: You run cells 1, 2 and 3 in that order, then run only cell 2 again. What is total now?
hints: Which value of rate does the kernel hold when cell 2 runs again?
Cell 3 changed rate before cell 2 ran the second time.
Work out 5 × 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The kernel holds rate = 5, so cell 2 gives 5 × 10 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: 50. Cell 2 read the newest rate the kernel held, so the result depends on the run order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is total from the first run. Cell 2 ran again, now with the newer rate.
That is only the multiplier. Multiply it by the rate the kernel holds.

questions.prompt: Set units = 6 and cost = 7, then calculate total = units * cost. What is total?
hints: Substitute both stored values.
The calculation multiplies the two names.
Work out 6 × 7.
questions.onCorrect: 42. The line reads the stored values of units and cost and multiplies them.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the values. The line uses *, which multiplies.

questions.prompt: A script sets x = 3, then x = x + 2, then y = x * 4. What is y?
hints: Follow the lines in order.
x changes before y is worked out.
Work out (3 + 2) × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line makes x equal 5; the last line gives 5 × 4 = 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. x = x + 2 stores 5 under x, and y then uses that new value.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the old x = 3. The second line changed x before y was calculated.
That is 3 + 2 + 4. The last line multiplies.

hints: Did cell 2 run again after the edit?
m was stored from the first run of cell 2.
Work out 3 + 4.
questions.prompt: Cell 1 sets k = 3 and cell 2 sets m = k + 4. You change cell 1 to k = 10 and run only cell 1. What is m now?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: m keeps 3 + 4 = 7 until cell 2 is run again.

questions.onCorrect: 7. m was stored when cell 2 last ran. Editing and running cell 1 does not recalculate it.

misconceptions.feedback: That recalculates with the new k. Cell 2 has not run again, so m still holds the older result.
That is the new k. The question asks for m.

hints: B1's formula refers to A1. What is in A1 now?
The formula multiplies A1 by 4.
Work out 9 × 4.
questions.prompt: What number does B1 show now?
questions.onCorrect: 36. A spreadsheet formula recalculates when its inputs change. Python assignments behave differently, as the next screens show.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B1 before the change. A spreadsheet formula recalculates when A1 changes.
That adds 4 instead of multiplying. The formula is =A1*4.

hints: Think about what happens when the line runs, not what it promises later.
questions.prompt: What does the line price = 4 do?

choices.label: Promises that price will always equal 4

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An assignment stores the value in the name once, when the line runs.

questions.onCorrect: It stores the value 4 under the name price. A later line can store a different value under the same name.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how a spreadsheet rule behaves. An assignment runs once; nothing keeps it true afterwards.
A question about equality uses a double equals sign. One equals sign stores a value.

hints: Where does the second run get its starting value from?
questions.prompt: Why does the second run give 8 rather than 5?

choices.label: The kernel kept count = 5 from the first run.
Each run starts again from the first cell.

acceptedIdeas: The kernel kept count = 5 from the first run.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kernel keeps names between cell runs, so each run starts from the last value.

questions.onCorrect: The kernel kept count = 5, so the second run adds 3 to that.

misconceptions.feedback: Then every run would give 5. The kernel does not rewind between runs.
The statement adds 3 to whatever count holds. The result depends on the starting value.

hints: Start from the value the kernel kept, 5.
Add 4 to it.
Work out 5 + 4.
questions.prompt: What is count after the second run?
questions.onCorrect: 9. Each run adds 4 to whatever the kernel kept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value after the first run. The second run adds 4 more.
That is only the amount added. Add it to the kept value.
